transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-16 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Graves (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Sequoia Head of SRE), Liam O'Neal (Sequoia VP Eng), Jordan Ramos (Sequoia Oncall)

Summary:
- Quick synthesis of the incident on 2026-03-12 where customer saw sustained 5xx spike and degraded latency for ~45 minutes.
- Agreed hypothesis: aggressive eviction behavior + KV cache mismatch + model variant fallback thrash.
- Short-term mitigations: Dedicated fallback pool, increase kv-cache retention, conservative autoscale thresholds.
- Long-term: joint runbook, chaos testing, telemetry augmentation, audit of quantized model variants.

Topics covered:
- Incident timeline and key metrics (p50/p95/p99, token throughput)
- Root-cause hypothesis: eviction vs OOM vs quantization mismatch
- Trade-offs: latency cost vs dedicated reserve vs degradation tolerance
- Compliance/logging requirements and evidence capture for auditors
- Next steps and owners

Action items (read out): Sofia reads action list, customer confirms owners.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick nod, we'll run 50 minutes, capture actions. Ethan and I will drive tech details.
[00:22] Maya (Sequoia): Yeah thanks, we had a rough weekend, so appreciate you fitting this in. we forwarded the initial incident timeline to the shared folder, hope you saw that.
[00:35] Ethan (Redwood SE): Yep saw it, thanks Maya. we pulled some of your trace spans but the correlating ids on a few spans were truncated, so we want the raw export if possible.
[00:45] Liam (Sequoia): we can get that, jordan's already lined up to pull k8s events and dmesg, but we need to be careful with PII in traces.
[00:58] Jordan (Oncall): quick note - during the spike we did an emergency rollback to previous model and that dropped the 5xx but latency stayed a bit elevated. not sure if the rollback caused more cache churn.
[01:15] Ethan: Right, that's consistent with a kv-cache warmup problem. when you rollback model weights the kv keys don't line up sometimes, and you get extra token recompute. we call it kv mismatch - it's an area we have heuristics for but not perfect.
[01:36] Maya: the weird thing was eviction alarms firing - we saw a lot of LRU evicts across the fleet. memory looked okay overall but transient pressure spiked.
[01:48] Sofia: Can you walk us through your autoscaler signals? hi-level: what triggered additional nodes and what was the cooldown?
[02:03] Liam: our HPA is based on cpu and custom token-per-second metric. cooldown is 120s. during the incident we saw a bunch of bursty traffic from a partner batch job which seems to have created hot paths.
[02:20] Ethan: big picture - bursty traffic plus model rollback equals kv cache misses plus bursty tensor allocation. that combination will cause evictions and token regen pressure.
[02:35] Jordan: there's also an oddity, we had one AZ report a higher eviction rate; the others were lower. could be a node flavor mismatch, we moved some spot nodes in to handle cost.
[02:50] Sofia: that ties to the Dedicated vs Hosted conversation we had last week. If you had a small reserved pool with pinned instance types, it reduces instance heterogeneity and eviction surprises.
[03:08] Maya: yeah the cost team hates reserved pools though. we need a clear unit economics picture.
[03:15] Liam: also curious about the runtime - is there a known issue with the new quantized variant we onboarded?
[03:28] Ethan: good question. we did ship a 4-bit quant variant recently; it's generally stable but there's a corner case with non-matching kv schema after fast rollbacks. it's called an intermediate cache key schema change. transcription note: ethan says "kv schema", sometimes shows up as "k v schema" in traces.
[03:48] Maya: so could a rollback to an older param set cause the model to produce different cache keys?
[03:55] Ethan: yes, if tokenization or past-context encoding changes slightly, keys differ and cache hits plummet. then requests regenerate history which spends cycles and can cause timeouts.
[04:10] Jordan: during the incident, we saw increased tail latency on calls that hit the edge router, with a backlog building at the gateway.
[04:25] Sofia: Did the gateway have circuit breakers?
[04:29] Jordan: yes but the default threshold was too high; it closed late. we have an open PR to tune it but it wasn't deployed.
[04:40] Liam: can we get a reproducible test? even a scaled synthetic job that mimics the partner batch traffic.
[04:50] Ethan: absolutely. We'll script a workload that simulates token distribution and rolling model swaps to stress eviction and kv warmup. we'll run it in your staging.
[05:05] Maya: that would help. also want to understand the logs we need to keep for auditors — e.g, HIPAA-ish stuff for a vertical customer — we need to show trace retention and access controls.
[05:20] Sofia: Redwood's private offering supports VPC + KMS and audit logs; we'll share SOC2 artifacts. transcription glitch: customer heard "SOX two" earlier but it's SOC 2.
[05:36] Liam: perfect, we need that pack urgently.
[05:40] Ethan: on mitigation options: short-term we recommend enabling a small warm standby pool (dedicated reserve) and bumping kv-cache TTL/retention to keep more keys. medium-term we propose runbook + chaos test, and long-term we want an integration that validates kv key stability across model rollouts.
[06:02] Jordan: what about falling back to a smaller model variant? We used a tiny model for a minute and that helped but output quality dropped.
[06:14] Ethan: fallback to smaller model is fine as a safety net if the app can tolerate some quality regression. we can set a graceful degrade policy in the router that prefers low-latency cheap variants when token queue depth spikes.
[06:30] Maya: the product team will want explicit SLO targets and cost impact for the fallback.
[06:36] Sofia: We'll put together a tradeoff slide: p95 cost delta, expected token-per-second capacity, and latency uplift.
[06:45] Liam: also we've noticed an unexpected behavior in our autoscaler when ephemeral pods evict - the horizontal pod autoscaler doesn't immediately replace because of pending pod GC.
[06:57] Ethan: that's kubernetes kubelet eviction + cloud provider interplay; we can add a mitigation doc about draining and node replacement speed, and recommend node warmup.
[07:10] Jordan: small aside — logging amplification: during the incident we saw logs balloon, we had to throttle ingestion which delayed visibility.
[07:22] Sofia: that's a telemetry gap we want to fix. adding sampling or early filtering helps. also we'll propose a low-cost streaming aggregator so you get tail alerts without full ingest cost.
[07:40] Maya: may we also get a list of exact metrics and dashboards you want us to share? we'll produce them.
[07:48] Ethan: yes, we'll email a minimal observability checklist: token queue depth, kv hit ratio, eviction rate, p95/gateway queue length, per-model cached keys.
[07:59] Liam: can we annotate which metrics are critical for auditors? some of these might be sensitive.
[08:06] Sofia: we can mark them as operational vs forensic and propose retention windows.
[08:12] Maya: good.
[08:18] Ethan: I want to call out a small code-level artifact we saw: in your rollout pipeline there's a step that unpins the cache key version before the new artifact finishes loading. that transient window can cause mismatch.
[08:35] Jordan: that's in our deploy script. we can add a gating check to ensure the new model warmed before swapping keys.
[08:43] Ethan: exactly. we can provide a small plugin for your pipeline or a snippet.
[08:50] Liam: what's the remediation timeline we should budget for? if we accept dedicated fallback and one runbook rehearsal, when can we expect reduced risk?
[09:02] Sofia: With 2 weeks of work — dedicated pool config, kv retention bump, and a single chaos run — you should see significant reduction in long-tail 5xx events. we'll aim for 2-3 week mitigation window.
[09:18] Maya: that's acceptable if we have clear checkpoints.
[09:23] Ethan: for the chaos run, we propose three experiments: bursty partner traffic, rapid model rollbacks, and node flavor substitution. we'll capture evictions and token regen.
[09:36] Jordan: can you also run a controlled eviction only test? replicate LRU evicts at scale.
[09:42] Ethan: yes, that's part of the plan.
[09:46] Sofia: let's talk about cost: Dedicated fallback pool is roughly X% of your current spend for Y% increased availability. we'll quantify exact numbers and include in the next doc.
[09:58] Liam: The finance team will want net present cost for the quarter.
[10:02] Sofia: We'll include a quarterly delta and a three-month burn estimate.
[10:08] Maya: security/compliance question — if we enable a dedicated pool, does that change our data residency or audit posture?
[10:17] Ethan: no, dedicated pool can be provisioned in your VPC region and inherit KMS, so audit posture can improve. we'll provide a mapping doc.
[10:27] Liam: Thanks. Also curious about fallback model quality gating — can we add a canary evaluation before switching traffic?
[10:33] Ethan: yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback if metric regressions are detected. we'll show you how to configure thresholds for small-batch canaries.
[10:10] [note: timestamp drift - speaker timing jumps, typical transcription artifact]
[10:48] Jordan: small nit: we saw a burst caused by a partner's misconfigured job that retried on 429; question - can Redwood throttle per-API-key?
[10:57] Sofia: yes per-key rate limiting and token quotas are supported. we can scope those to partners or IPs.
[11:06] Liam: okay good, that may be a quick-win to reduce noisy neighbors.
[11:12] Ethan: back to root cause, our preliminary hypothesis list: 1) kv cache mismatch after rollback, 2) transient memory pressure causing aggressive LRU eviction, 3) heterogenous node types leading to local hot spots. we'll rank these and run tests to disambiguate.
[11:32] Maya: agree. can you include a prioritized test plan?
[11:36] Ethan: yes. We'll send a 1-page matrix mapping test -> hypothesis -> expected signal.
[11:44] Sofia: we'll also prepare a short comms template you can use internally to explain outage cause and mitigation to executives.
[11:54] Liam: that would be helpful.
[12:00] Maya: about auditors again — we need to show change control for model rollouts, do you have recommended policy templates?
[12:09] Ethan: we do. we'll share a model release checklist and an audit log sample.
[12:16] Jordan: what's the intended cadence for follow-up? weekly sync or ad hoc?
[12:22] Sofia: let's do weekly 30-minute sync until closure and a full runbook rehearsal after the mitigation work. schedule invite for next Monday same time?
[12:31] Maya: next Monday works for us.
[12:34] Sofia: great. final quick recap of immediate asks: Maya uploads traces, Jordan timeline, Ethan runs staging tests and shares plan, Sofia sends pricing and SOC2 artifacts. any other items?
[12:50] Liam: not from me.
[12:53] Maya: nothing more. thanks.
[12:56] Sofia: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs. end.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-attribution and timestamp drift; some product names munged (e.g., "Red wood Optimize" or "kv cache" split). There was light crosstalk and filler words.

References shared in chat: https://drive.redwood.example.com/incident-2026-03-12 (RCA draft), https://drive.redwood.example.com/observability-checklist, pricing addendum (sent after call).

End of transcript.
